raw:
**Move note.** Red opened by driving a piece from (0,3) straight into the centre at (3,3), so the fight for the four central squares — (3,3), (3,4), (4,3), (4,4) — starts immediately. I don't want to let Team A build up there unopposed, but I also don't want to hand them a free capture: the natural-looking (3,4) is a trap, because Red already sits at (3,3) and can drop a piece from (0,5) straight down to (3,5), sandwiching my piece on the very next move.

So I take the centre square directly *below* Red instead. Blue slides from (4,7) all the way along the open fourth row to (4,3). Three things recommend it:

1. It puts a Blue piece on a centre square, halving Team A's progress toward the four-square win.
2. It creates a real threat. Red at (3,3) is now pinned between my piece at (4,3) and the empty square (2,3). My next Blue turn can play (2,7) → (2,3) along the equally open second row, which sandwiches R(3,3) between two Blues and captures it. Red has to spend their turn answering that.
3. It is safe for now. To sandwich my piece at (4,3), Red needs matching Red pieces at either (4,2) and (4,4), or at (3,3) and (5,3). They own (3,3), but column 3 below it is unreachable in one move — their own piece blocks the column, and no Red piece stands on row 5 — so (5,3) costs them two turns. The horizontal pair costs two turns as well. Yellow cannot help with any of this: a sandwich needs both flanking pieces to be the *same* colour, so Red and Yellow can never combine to capture, and neither can my Blue and Green.

The longer-term shape I'm aiming for: keep Blue and Green from lining up adjacent to each other in an open row or column, since one enemy pair could then sweep up both of my colours in a single mixed-line sandwich. I'd rather approach the centre from two different axes.

raw:
**Move note.** Yellow answered by dropping (7,4) straight up to (4,4), so the centre is now split two-and-two: Red on (3,3), Yellow on (4,4), my Blue on (4,3), and (3,4) still empty.

The urgent thing is a threat I have to see one move ahead. My Blue on (4,3) already has Yellow sitting on its right at (4,4). If Yellow can also reach (4,2), my piece is sandwiched between two Yellows and dies — and (7,2) has a completely clear run up column 2 to (4,2). That capture is available to them on their very next turn.

I have three ways to stop it, and two of them are bad. Moving Blue off (4,3) surrenders a centre square and my whole plan. Plugging (4,2) with a Green piece looks natural but is actually worse than doing nothing: Green on (4,2) next to Blue on (4,3) forms a mixed two-piece line in row 4, and since a sandwich captures *every* piece in the line regardless of colour, Yellow simply plays (7,1) up to (4,1) and takes my Green and my Blue together, against the Yellow already standing on (4,4). One move, two pieces. This is exactly the Blue-Green adjacency I said I wanted to avoid.

So instead I block the road rather than the doorstep. Green runs from (5,0) to (5,2), planting itself in column 2 below the critical square. Now (7,2) can only get as far as (6,2); no Yellow piece can reach (4,2) from row 4 either, because Y(4,4)'s path left is blocked by my own Blue. The threat is dead without putting two of my pieces side by side.

What this preserves is the point. Red's piece on (3,3) is still trapped between my Blue on (4,3) and the empty (2,3), and row 2 is wide open from (2,7). Unless Red spends this turn running that piece away, my next Blue move is (2,7) to (2,3), sandwiching and capturing it for free. Red is more or less forced to retreat from the centre.

One thing I'm noting for later: pulling a piece out of my Green wall leaves a gap at (5,0), which means the four Greens on rows 1-4 are now a single unbroken line that could in principle be swept if one enemy colour ever held both (0,0) and (5,0). That's three moves away and easy to break up, but I'll keep watch on it.

raw:
**Move note.** Red has escalated: (0,4) ran down to (3,4), so Team A now holds three of the four centre squares — (3,3) and (3,4) in Red, (4,4) in Yellow. My Blue on (4,3) is the single piece standing between them and an instant centre victory. Everything now revolves around that square.

To take (4,3) they must first capture the piece sitting on it, and a sandwich needs two flankers of the *same* colour. There are exactly two flanking pairs: (4,2)+(4,4), which is Yellow's route, and (3,3)+(5,3), which is Red's. Yellow already owns (4,4) but cannot reach (4,2) — my Green on (5,2) plugs column 2, and Y(4,4)'s path leftward runs into my own Blue. Red already owns (3,3) and needs (5,3), which is currently two moves away since column 3 below their piece is blocked by my Blue and no Red piece stands on row 5.

So I take Red's half of that pincer off the board. Blue runs the whole open second row from (2,7) to (2,3). Looking down from the landing square, (3,3) is a Red piece and immediately beyond it is my own Blue on (4,3) — flanked by two Blues, so Red's centre piece is captured. Red's first loss, and I need only three to eliminate a colour.

The gain is bigger than one piece. It cuts Team A from three centre squares back to two, and it deletes precisely the flanker Red needed to ever pry my Blue off (4,3). After this, Red must spend a move re-occupying (3,3) — moving into a sandwich is safe, so I can't punish that directly — and only *then* start the two-move trek to (5,3). Yellow, meanwhile, still has no path to (4,2) at all.

I checked that nothing of mine is caught in the crossfire: the captured line is the single Red piece, with no teammate pieces mixed in, and none of my own pieces sit in a line that this landing completes.

The formation I'm left with — Blue on (2,3) and Blue on (4,3) with a hole at (3,3) — is deliberately shaped. Column 3 is now mine at both ends of the centre, and the two Blues mutually guard the approaches without ever standing adjacent to a Green, which is the pattern that would let one enemy sweep take two of my pieces at once. My watch list stays short: keep (4,3) occupied at all costs, and keep Red away from (5,3).

raw:
**Move note.** Yellow has committed to the plan I was watching for: (7,3) came up to (5,3), directly beneath my Blue on (4,3). That square is the whole game right now — Team A holds (3,4) and (4,4), and the moment they own both (3,3) and (4,3) they win outright. Yellow now has one half of the pincer that takes my Blue: they need Yellow on (3,3) and Yellow on (5,3), and they've just placed the second one.

So the question is how Yellow gets a piece to (3,3). I traced every route. Column 3 is sealed by my own Blues at (2,3) and (4,3). Column 2 is sealed by my Green on (5,2). Coming in along row 3 from the right doesn't work either, because Red's own piece on (3,4) blocks the way — their centre piece is in their partner's path. That leaves exactly one highway: column 1, where (7,1) has a clear run up to row 3 and can then slide across to (3,3).

Green plugs it. (4,0) steps one square right to (4,1), and column 1 is cut in half. Yellow's (7,1) can now reach only (5,1) and (6,1), and from there row 5 is blocked by my Green on (5,2) and column 0 by my Green on (6,0). Yellow is walled into the bottom-left with no path to row 3 at all. With that, my Blue on (4,3) is safe from both colours: Yellow can't reach (3,3) or (4,2), and Red can't use the (3,3)+(5,3) pincer because (5,3) is a *Yellow* piece — the two enemy colours can never combine for a sandwich.

The same little step solves a structural worry I flagged two turns ago. Pulling pieces out of my left wall was leaving the remaining Greens as one long unbroken line that could be swept if Red ever held both ends of it. By moving from (4,0) rather than deeper, the surviving line is rows 1-3, and its lower end (4,0) sits behind my new blocker — Red can't come down column 1 past (4,1) to reach row 5 and work around. The wall is no longer sweepable.

I also deliberately kept row 6 clear rather than developing Green along it, because that row is my next attack. Yellow's piece on (5,3) is already half-trapped: my Green on (5,2) sits on its left, and my Blue on (4,3) sits above it. Next turn Blue runs (6,7) all the way to (6,3), and looking up from there the Yellow piece is flanked by Blue above — captured. If Red spends this turn throwing a blocker onto row 6 to stop that, they'll have spent a move on pure defence while I keep building, and I still have a slower route to the same capture by bringing Green around to (5,4).

That takes Yellow from one loss to three, which eliminates the colour. Red was already eliminated four moves ago. Both colours of Team A are gone, which is team elimination and the game.

The shape came from patience rather than a single trick. Early on I fixed on the fact that a centre victory needs all four central squares, so holding just one of them — and making it genuinely untakeable — shuts that win condition off entirely. My Blue on (4,3) did that job for most of the game, protected by Greens on (4,2) and (5,3) sitting on the exact squares an enemy would have needed to flank from. You can't be flanked from a square you're standing on, and the two enemy colours can never pair up for a sandwich, so Red owning (3,3) and Yellow owning (4,4) never combined into anything.

The other thread was the fork that finished Red: a Green to (1,2) created two separate capture threats, on (3,4) and on (3,2), with only one Red turn between them. Red had no move that answered both, and once they fell to three losses their survivors turned to Void — moving, blocking, but permanently unable to capture. From that point only Yellow could threaten anything, and Yellow needed two of its own pieces for every capture.

The finish was Yellow's own doing. Placing (4,4) and (4,5) side by side next to my Blue on (4,3) built the line for me; all I needed was to walk a piece down the empty column 7 to (4,7) and take (4,6). When they answered by sending (5,6) up to (2,6) instead of breaking the line or plugging the square, it was over — and their own pieces on (4,4) and (4,5) were blocking the only columns their Void Red pieces could have used to reach (4,6) in time.

Final tally: Red eliminated, Yellow eliminated, Blue lost one piece, Green lost none.
